claim: The principle of efficient coding posits that sensory cortical networks are designed to encode maximal sensory information with minimal metabolic cost.
source: The principle of efficient coding posits that sensory cortical networks are designed to encode maximal sensory information with minimal metabolic cost.
evidence: This is a statement of the efficient coding principle as presented in the abstract, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The optimal network has biologically plausible biophysical features, including realistic integrate-and-fire spiking dynamics, spike-triggered adaptation, and a non-specific excitatory external input.
source: The optimal network has biologically plausible biophysical features, including realistic integrate-and-fire spiking dynamics, spike-triggered adaptation, and a non-specific excitatory external input.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analytical derivation presented in the manuscript and the model parameters shown in Table 1.

claim: The excitatory-inhibitory recurrent connectivity between neurons with similar stimulus tuning implements feature-specific competition, similar to that recently found in visual cortex.
source: The excitatory-inhibitory recurrent connectivity between neurons with similar stimulus tuning implements feature-specific competition, similar to that recently found in visual cortex.
evidence: This is supported by the photostimulation experiments described in the manuscript and comparison with empirical findings.

claim: Networks with unstructured connectivity cannot reach comparable levels of coding efficiency.
source: Networks with unstructured connectivity cannot reach comparable levels of coding efficiency.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing structured and unstructured networks in Figure 4.

claim: The optimal ratio of excitatory vs inhibitory neurons and the ratio of mean inhibitory-to-inhibitory vs excitatory-to-inhibitory connectivity are comparable to those of cortical sensory networks.
source: The optimal ratio of excitatory vs inhibitory neurons and the ratio of mean inhibitory-to-inhibitory vs excitatory-to-inhibitory connectivity are comparable to those of cortical sensory networks.
evidence: This is supported by the parameter optimization results shown in Figure 7 and Table 1, compared against empirical measurements.

claim: The efficient network solution exhibits an instantaneous balance between excitation and inhibition.
source: The efficient network solution exhibits an instantaneous balance between excitation and inhibition.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the correlation analysis of synaptic inputs shown in Figure 1I and discussed throughout the manuscript.

claim: The network can perform efficient coding even when external stimuli vary over multiple time scales.
source: The network can perform efficient coding even when external stimuli vary over multiple time scales.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis in Figure 8A-B showing stable performance across different stimulus timescales.

claim: Efficient coding has been highly influential as a normative theory of how networks are organized and designed to optimally process natural sensory stimuli in visual (Atick, 1992; Olshausen and Field, 1997; Simoncelli and Olshausen, 2001; Vinje and Gallant, 2000; Olshausen and Field, 2004; Li, 2014), auditory (Lewicki, 2002), and olfactory sensory pathways (Koulakov and Rinberg, 2011).
source: Efficient coding has been highly influential as a normative theory of how networks are organized and designed to optimally process natural sensory stimuli in visual (Atick, 1992; Olshausen and Field, 1997; Simoncelli and Olshausen, 2001; Vinje and Gallant, 2000; Olshausen and Field, 2004; Li, 2014), auditory (Lewicki, 2002), and olfactory sensory pathways (Koulakov and Rinberg, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work on efficient coding in different sensory modalities.

claim: Biological networks often encode information through millisecond-precise spike timing (Bialek et al., 1991; Bialek and Rieke, 1992; Panzeri et al., 2001; Nemenman et al., 2008; Kayser et al., 2010; Ince et al., 2013; Panzeri et al., 2010).
source: Instead, biological networks often encode information through millisecond-precise spike timing (Bialek et al., 1991; Bialek and Rieke, 1992; Panzeri et al., 2001; Nemenman et al., 2008; Kayser et al., 2010; Ince et al., 2013; Panzeri et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an established finding in neuroscience supported by multiple citations.

claim: The network is composed of 400 E and 100 I units, a network size relevant for computations within one layer of a cortical microcolumn (Lefort et al., 2009).
source: The numerical optimization was performed by simulating a model of 400 E and 100 I units, a network size relevant for computations within one layer of a cortical microcolumn (Lefort et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lefort et al., 2009 and is used as justification for the network size chosen.

claim: I neurons had higher average firing rates compared to E neurons, consistently with observations in cortex (Neske et al., 2015).
source: I neurons had higher average firing rates compared to E neurons, consistently with observations in cortex (Neske et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data and comparison with empirical observations cited.

claim: The distribution of firing rates was well described by a log-normal distribution, consistent with distributions of cortical firing observed empirically (Buzsáki and Mizuseki, 2014).
source: The distribution of firing rates was well described by a log-normal distribution (Figure 1F, left), consistent with distributions of cortical firing observed empirically (Buzsáki and Mizuseki, 2014).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 1F and compared against empirical findings.

claim: Neurons fired irregularly, with mean coefficient of variation (CV) slightly smaller than 1 (CV = [0.97, 0.95] for E and I neurons, respectively), compatible with cortical firing (Softky and Koch, 1993).
source: Neurons fired irregularly, with mean coefficient of variation (CV) slightly smaller than 1 (Figure 1F, right; CV = [0.97, 0.95] for E and I neurons, respectively), compatible with cortical firing (Softky and Koch, 1993).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from simulations shown in Figure 1F and compared with empirical observations.

claim: The photostimulation of the target E neuron increased the instantaneous firing rate of similarly-tuned I neurons and reduced that of other similarly-tuned E neurons.
source: The photostimulation of the target E neuron increased the instantaneous firing rate of similarly-tuned I neurons and reduced that of other similarly-tuned E neurons (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulated photostimulation experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The optimal network replicates the preponderance of negative effective connectivity between E neurons and the dependence of its strength on tuning similarity found in Chettih and Harvey, 2019.
source: Thus, the optimal network replicates the preponderance of negative effective connectivity between E neurons and the dependence of its strength on tuning similarity found in Chettih and Harvey, 2019.
evidence: This is supported by the photostimulation simulation results and comparison with empirical findings.

claim: Structured networks differ from unstructured ones by showing better encoding performance, lower metabolic cost, weaker variance of the membrane potential over time, lower firing rates and weaker average and instantaneous balance of synaptic inputs.
source: In particular, structured networks differ from unstructured ones by showing better encoding performance (Figure 4A), lower metabolic cost (Figure 4B), weaker variance of the membrane potential over time (Figure 4C), lower firing rates (Figure 4D) and weaker average (Figure 4F) and instantaneous balance (Figure 4G) of synaptic inputs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing structured and unstructured networks across multiple measures shown in Figure 4.

claim: The optimally efficient solution does not include within-neuron feedback, while a model with weak and short-lasting spike-triggered adaptation is slightly suboptimal, although still highly efficient.
source: In sum, our results show that the optimally efficient solution does not include within-neuron feedback, while a model with weak and short-lasting spike-triggered adaptation is slightly suboptimal, although still highly efficient.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of spike-triggered adaptation shown in Figure 5.

claim: The optimal efficiency was achieved for non-zero levels of the metabolic constant.
source: The optimal efficiency was achieved for non-zero levels of the metabolic constant (Figure 6B), with the mean of the non-specific current spanning more than half of the distance between the resting potential and the threshold (Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the parameter optimization shown in Figure 6B and the optimal parameters in Table 1.

claim: The optimal performance was achieved with non-vanishing noise levels, similarly to previous work showing that the noise prevents excessive network synchronization that would harm performance (Chalk et al., 2016; Koren and Denève, 2017; Timcheck et al., 2022).
source: The optimal performance was achieved with non-vanishing noise levels (Figure 6F), similarly to previous work showing that the noise prevents excessive network synchronization that would harm performance (Chalk et al., 2016; Koren and Denève, 2017; Timcheck et al., 2022).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6F and supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claim: A decrease of the number of I neurons (and thus an increase in the ratio of the number of E to I neurons) caused a linear increase in the firing rate of I neurons, while the firing rate of E neurons stayed constant.
source: As predicted, a decrease of the number of I neurons (and thus an increase in the ratio of the number of E to I neurons) caused a linear increase in the firing rate of I neurons, while the firing rate of E neurons stayed constant (Figure 7B, top).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Network efficiency was maximized when the ratio of mean I-I to E-I efficacy was about 3:1.
source: Network efficiency was maximized when such ratio was about 3–1 (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the parameter optimization shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Our results suggest the optimal E-I and I-E synaptic efficacy, averaged across neuronal pairs, of 0.75 mV, and the optimal I-I efficacy of 2.25 mV, values that are consistent with empirical measurements in the primary sensory cortex (Cossell et al., 2015; Pala and Petersen, 2015; Campagnola et al., 2022).
source: Our results suggest the optimal E-I and I-E synaptic efficacy, averaged across neuronal pairs, of 0.75 mV, and the optimal I-I efficacy of 2.25 mV, values that are consistent with empirical measurements in the primary sensory cortex (Cossell et al., 2015; Pala and Petersen, 2015; Campagnola et al., 2022).
evidence: This is derived from the model parameters and compared against empirical measurements.

claim: The network efficiently encoded stimulus features when their time constants varied between 1 and 200 ms, with stable encoding error, metabolic cost and neural dynamics.
source: The network efficiently encoded stimulus features when their time constants varied between 1 and 200 ms, with stable encoding error, metabolic cost (Figure 8A) and neural dynamics (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figure 8A and supplementary figures.

claim: Compared to the 1CT model, the E-I model exhibited a higher encoding error and metabolic cost in the E population, but a lower encoding error and metabolic cost in the I population.
source: Compared to the 1CT model, the E-I model exhibited a higher encoding error and metabolic cost in the E population, but a lower encoding error and metabolic cost in the I population (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison between models shown in Figure 8G.

claim: The 1CT model is slightly more efficient than the E population of the E-I model, consistently for different weightings of the error with the cost.
source: We found that the 1CT model is slightly more efficient than the E population of the E-I model, consistently for different weightings of the error with the cost (Figure 8H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison shown in Figure 8H.

claim: Firing rates in the 1CT model were highly sensitive to variations in the metabolic constant, with a superexponential growth of the firing rate with the inverse of the metabolic constant in regimes with metabolic cost lower than optimal.
source: Consistently with previous studies (Koren and Denève, 2017; Rullán Buxó and Pillow, 2020), firing rates in the 1CT model were highly sensitive to variations in the metabolic constant (Figure 8I, note the logarithmic scale on the y-axis), with a superexponential growth of the firing rate with the inverse of the metabolic constant in regimes with metabolic cost lower than optimal.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 8I and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The E-I model's firing rates exhibited lower sensitivity to the metabolic constant, and never exceeded physiological limits.
source: This is in contrast to the E-I model, whose firing rates exhibited lower sensitivity to the metabolic constant, and never exceeded physiological limits (Figure 7C, top).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the E-I model behavior shown in Figure 7C with the 1CT model behavior.

claim: The optimal parameters (including the ratio between the number of E and I neurons, the ratio of I-I to E-I synaptic efficacy and parameters of non-specific currents) were consistent with parameters measured empirically in cortical circuits.
source: The optimal parameters (including the ratio between the number of E and I neurons, the ratio of I-I to E-I synaptic efficacy and parameters of non-specific currents) were consistent with parameters measured empirically in cortical circuits, and generated plausible spiking dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by the parameter optimization results and comparisons with empirical data throughout the manuscript.

claim: I neurons develop stimulus feature selectivity because of the structured recurrent connectivity.
source: A first insight is that I neurons develop stimulus feature selectivity because of the structured recurrent connectivity.
evidence: This is an inference from the model structure and simulation results showing I neuron tuning.

claim: A network with structured connectivity shows stronger average and instantaneous E-I balance, as well as significantly lower variance of membrane potentials compared to an equivalent network with randomly organized connections.
source: A second insight is that a network with structured connectivity shows stronger average and instantaneous E-I balance, as well as significantly lower variance of membrane potentials compared to an equivalent network with randomly organized connections.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison between structured and unstructured networks shown in Figure 4.

claim: The structured network exhibits both lower encoding error and lower firing rates compared to unstructured networks, thus achieving higher efficiency.
source: A third insight is that the structured network exhibits both lower encoding error and lower firing rates compared to unstructured networks, thus achieving higher efficiency.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: The network has to have structured E-I and I-E connectivity and weak and short-lasting or no spike-triggered adaptation.
source: The network has to have structured E-I and I-E connectivity and weak and short-lasting or no spike-triggered adaptation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of connectivity structure and adaptation effects.

claim: At least half of the distance between the resting potential and the threshold should be provided by a stochastic external current that is unrelated to the feedforward stimuli.
source: Further, at least half of the distance between the resting potential and the threshold should be provided by a stochastic external current that is unrelated to the feedforward stimuli.
evidence: This is derived from the optimal model parameters shown in Table 1.

claim: The network should have a ratio of E to I neuron numbers in the range of about 2:1 to 4:1 and the ratio of average I-I to E-I connectivity in the range of about 2:1 to 3:1.
source: Finally, the network should have a ratio of E to I neuron numbers in the range of about 2:1 to 4:1 and the ratio of average I-I to E-I connectivity in the range of about 2:1 to 3:1, with smaller E-I neuron number ratios implying smaller average I-I to E-I connectivity ratios.
evidence: This is derived from the parameter optimization results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Moderate levels of E-I balance are optimal for coding, and too strong levels of instantaneous E-I balance are detrimental to coding efficiency.
source: Consistent with the general idea put forth in Deneve and Machens, 2016b; Chalk et al., 2016; Denève et al., 2017, we here showed that moderate levels of E-I balance are optimal for coding, and that too strong levels of instantaneous E-I balance are detrimental to coding efficiency.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of E-I balance and its relationship to network efficiency throughout the manuscript.

claim: Structured E-I-E connectivity is necessary for optimal levels of instantaneous E-I balance.
source: Our results predict that structured E-I-E connectivity is necessary for optimal levels of instantaneous E-I balance.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison of structured and unstructured networks in Figure 4.

claim: The E-I-E structured connectivity causes desynchronization of the spiking output.
source: Finally, the E-I-E structured connectivity that we derived supports optimal levels of instantaneous E-I balance and causes desynchronization of the spiking output.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the cross-correlogram analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The optima of the E-I neuron number ratio and the I-I to E-I connectivity ratio are positively correlated.
source: In particular, our analysis predicts that the optima of these two ratios are positively correlated.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the two-dimensional parameter search shown in Figure 7J.

claim: The efficient network does not require recurrent E-E connections.
source: We found that our efficient network, optimizing the representation of a leaky integration of stimulus features, does not require recurrent E-E connections.
evidence: This is a consequence of the model assumptions and analytical derivation.

claim: The connection probability of recurrent synapses is 0.5.
source: Rectification also sets the overall connection probability to 0.5, which is consistent with empirically observed connection probability from pyramidal (E) neurons to parvalbumin-positive (I) neurons (Pala and Petersen, 2015; Campagnola et al., 2022), but likely overestimates the connection probability from parvalbumin-positive neurons to pyramidal neurons, which tends to be lower (Campagnola et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a consequence of the rectification procedure and is compared against empirical measurements.

claim: The average firing rate of both cell types, as well as the variability of spiking in E neurons, increased with noise strength.
source: The average firing rate of both cell types, as well as the variability of spiking in E neurons, increased with noise strength (Figure 6G), and some level of noise in the non-specific inputs was necessary to establish the optimal level of spiking variability.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Significant levels of spiking variability were measured already in the absence of noise, with a coefficient of variation of about 0.8 in E and 0.9 in I neurons.
source: Nevertheless, we measured significant levels of spiking variability already in the absence of noise, with a coefficient of variation of about 0.8 in E and 0.9 in I neurons (Figure 6G, bottom).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from simulations shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The recurrent network dynamics generates substantial variability even in absence of an external source of noise.
source: This indicates that the recurrent network dynamics generates substantial variability even in absence of an external source of noise.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of spiking variability in the absence of external noise.

claim: The optima of the metabolic constant and the noise strength were positively correlated.
source: As expected, the optima of the metabolic constant and the noise strength were positively correlated.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the two-dimensional parameter search shown in Figure 6I.

claim: The model predicts that more than half of the average distance between the resting potential and firing threshold is accounted for by non-specific synaptic currents.
source: In qualitative agreement with empirical measurements (Destexhe and Paré, 1999; Destexhe et al., 2003), our model predicts that more than half of the average distance between the resting potential and firing threshold is accounted for by non-specific synaptic currents.
evidence: This is derived from the optimal model parameters and compared with empirical observations.

claim: Some level of external noise, in the form of a random fluctuation of the non-specific synaptic current, is beneficial for network efficiency.
source: Similarly to previous theoretical work (Chalk et al., 2016; Koren and Denève, 2017), we find that some level of external noise, in the form of a random fluctuation of the non-specific synaptic current, is beneficial for network efficiency.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the analysis in Figure 6F and supported by citations to previous work.
